strengths: The paper addresses an important practical setting: generating localized industrial anomalies without real defect samples, masks, or category-specific fine-tuning. The use of a normal reference also appropriately prioritizes preservation of product geometry and illumination.

The synchronized normal/anomalous diffusion branches provide an intuitive mechanism for obtaining an image-specific edit mask, and combining this with latent inpainting, anomaly-token attention biasing, and prompt refinement forms a coherent pipeline.

The downstream experiment is useful: synthetic data are used to train a U-Net and evaluated on real MVTec AD anomalies. DeltaDeno improves the zero-shot AnomalyAny mean results from 77.6/87.1/83.3/26.5 to 84.7/91.3/84.9/30.5 for image AUROC/AP and pixel AUROC/AP, respectively.

The ablation study indicates that inpainting, attention biasing, and prompt refinement each contribute to downstream performance. The qualitative examples also suggest reasonable background preservation and some prompt-dependent control over defect morphology.
The paper is generally well organized, appropriately acknowledges limitations such as difficulty with logical anomalies, and cites relevant diffusion editing and anomaly-generation literature.
weaknesses: The algorithm is internally inconsistent as written. Sampling begins at t_start=gamma*T with gamma=0.3 and T=100, hence at timestep 30, but the mask is said to be extracted at t_mid=floor(T/2)=50 after an early stage defined over [T,T/2]. That midpoint is never reached by a trajectory from 30 to 0. Moreover, Algorithm 1 places the t_mid branch after an early-stage condition that apparently includes t_mid, making that branch unreachable. This prevents faithful reproduction of the central two-stage procedure and leaves unclear what was actually evaluated.

The evidence does not substantiate the headline claims of precise localization and photorealism. There is no direct evaluation of generated-mask accuracy, boundary quality, foreground preservation, or similarity to real anomaly masks. Inception Score is poorly suited to measuring realism for small, class-specific industrial datasets, and IC-LPIPS measures diversity rather than realism. No human study, distributional metric against real defects, or preservation metric is provided.

Cross-category and cross-domain generalization is asserted more strongly than demonstrated. Quantitative experiments cover only MVTec AD, while evidence for unseen categories consists of a very limited qualitative figure. The additional datasets claimed to be in an appendix or supplement are absent from the supplied manuscript.

Originality appears limited relative to DiffEdit and related editing methods: prompt-conditioned denoising differences for mask construction, source-image partial noising, mask-based latent blending, and cross-attention manipulation are established ideas. Accumulating latent-trajectory differences for anomaly generation is a relevant adaptation, but the paper does not carefully isolate how it differs technically or empirically from a direct DiffEdit-style baseline.

Important implementation details are missing, including classifier-free guidance scale, beta for attention biasing, prompt-refinement iterations and alpha/lambda/eta, smoothing and mask-cleaning operations, SAM configuration, anomaly-token selection under subword tokenization, prompt lists, U-Net training details, and repeated-run statistics. Saying that remaining settings follow standard Stable Diffusion is insufficient because several central components have no standard configuration.

The proposed context loss pulls every non-anomaly token toward their within-prompt mean rather than aligning corresponding shared tokens between the normal and anomalous prompts. This can collapse semantically distinct token embeddings and does not mathematically implement the claimed normal/anomaly context alignment. No focused ablation or analysis validates this design.

The downstream results are reported without uncertainty across seeds, and the comparison protocol is insufficiently documented. Only DeltaDeno and AnomalyAny are explicitly controlled to use the same single normal source image, leaving comparability with the other methods unclear. The claim of consistent superiority is also overstated: DeltaDeno loses to AnomalyAny on some category/metric combinations, such as cable pixel AP.

The method uses two diffusion trajectories, 100 denoising steps, SAM, embedding optimization, and attention modification, yet supplies no runtime or memory evaluation. This is important given the paper's practical framing and its criticism of prior zero-shot inference as slow. Overall, the promising idea and results are outweighed by a central algorithmic inconsistency and inadequate validation of localization, realism, generalization, and reproducibility.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important setting: generating localized industrial anomalies without real defect examples or generator fine-tuning.

The proposed pipeline is intuitively motivated. Normal-reference initialization, anomaly localization, mask-constrained latent editing, and paired image/mask output could be useful for data bootstrapping.

The evaluation includes all 15 MVTec AD categories, comparisons with both zero-shot and few-shot generators, downstream detection metrics, and module-level ablations. The reported mean downstream gains over AnomalyAny are substantial.
weaknesses: There is a fundamental inconsistency in the sampling schedule. The method defines t_start=gamma*T, uses gamma=0.3, and samples from t_start to zero, but sets t_mid=floor(T/2) and describes the early stage as T to T/2. With T=100, sampling begins at 30 and can never reach the stated midpoint at 50, so the mask-extraction and stage-switching procedure cannot execute as written. This makes the central algorithm unreproducible and may indicate a deeper mismatch between the equations and experiments.

The main localization idea is insufficiently distinguished from DiffEdit, which also obtains an edit mask by contrasting source- and target-prompt diffusion predictions under shared noise. DeltaDeno combines this concept with established masked latent blending, attention biasing, and prompt-embedding optimization, but provides neither a precise analysis of the novelty relative to DiffEdit nor a DiffEdit-based baseline or ablation.

The description of delta attribution is internally inconsistent: the abstract says it contrasts denoiser predictions, whereas Eq. 8 compares post-update latents from two independently evolving trajectories. Once those trajectories diverge, their difference need not isolate anomaly semantics. No comparison against evaluating both prompts on the same latent, no localization accuracy against real masks, and no analysis validating the attribution interpretation are provided.

The generation-quality evidence is weak. Inception Score is not a reliable measure of realism for small, specialized industrial categories, while IC-LPIPS measures diversity but can reward artifacts. There is no FID/KID against real anomalies, precision-recall-style generative metric, human study, or quantitative background-preservation and mask-fidelity evaluation. The mean IS advantage over AnomalyAny is only 2.03 versus 2.02, and DeltaDeno loses on IS in several categories, contrary to the broad superiority claims.

The downstream study lacks uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, seed information, prompt lists, normal-image selection rules, U-Net training details, and sensitivity analysis. Generating all samples from a single unspecified normal image per category can introduce strong selection bias. The method is also worse than AnomalyAny on several individual categories, including cable, capsule, grid, and metal nut, so the claim of consistent gains is overstated.

Several essential implementation details are missing or questionable. The construction of the detailed semantic anchor is not specified; multi-token anomalies are not handled; mask resizing across different cross-attention resolutions is omitted; and thresholds and attention/refinement hyperparameters lack sensitivity studies. Moreover, L_ctx collapses non-anomaly token embeddings toward their own centroid rather than aligning them with the corresponding normal-prompt tokens, which does not match the stated motivation and may destroy token semantics.

The qualitative evaluation is too limited to support cross-domain generalization: it shows only a handful of examples and one vaguely described category outside MVTec AD, with no dataset provenance, systematic evaluation, failure cases, or comparison to real defects. Masks are displayed only as small insets, making boundary-quality claims difficult to assess.

Reproducibility is presently poor: code is only promised, many settings are deferred to unspecified 'standard Stable Diffusion' configuration or supplementary material, and compute cost is not reported despite requiring two diffusion branches, 100 denoising steps, SAM, prompt optimization, and repeated attention modification. Overall, the idea has merit, but the algorithmic contradiction and inadequate validation leave the scientific case unconvincing.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical setting: generating localized industrial anomalies without real anomalous samples, masks, or model fine-tuning. This is a meaningful computer-vision contribution under the default Algorithms/General category.

DeltaDeno presents a coherent combination of synchronized normal/anomalous diffusion branches, accumulated latent discrepancies, mask-guided inpainting, token refinement, and anomaly-token-specific attention biasing. The image-conditioned attribution mask is intuitive and potentially useful beyond anomaly generation.

The downstream experiment provides encouraging evidence of practical utility. Against the directly comparable zero-shot AnomalyAny baseline, DeltaDeno improves mean image AUROC from 77.6 to 84.7, image AP from 87.1 to 91.3, pixel AUROC from 83.3 to 84.9, and pixel AP from 26.5 to 30.5.

The component ablation is directionally convincing: removing inpainting, attention biasing, or prompt refinement reduces all reported downstream metrics. The qualitative examples also suggest good preservation of non-defective regions and some prompt-based control over defect morphology.

The presentation is generally clear, with a helpful pipeline diagram, algorithm summary, category-wise results, and an honest limitations section acknowledging limited fine-grained control and difficulty with logical anomalies.
weaknesses: There is a significant inconsistency in the timestep specification. Section 3 defines the early stage as t in [T,T/2] and extracts the intermediate mask at t_mid=floor(T/2), but initialization uses t_start=gamma*T and the reported gamma is 0.3. Sampling from 0.3T to 0 therefore never reaches T/2. Algorithm 1 and the equations consequently do not specify an executable procedure without reinterpretation, materially affecting reproducibility.

The evidence for the central claims of precise localization and photorealism is incomplete. No direct mask-quality metric against MVTec ground truth is reported, while IS is a weak realism measure for narrow industrial categories and IC-LPIPS measures diversity rather than correctness. Human evaluation, precision/recall-style generative metrics, boundary measures, or direct mask IoU/AUPRO would substantially strengthen the case.

Experimental coverage is narrow: quantitative results are confined to MVTec AD, while cross-category or cross-domain generalization is supported only by a few qualitative unseen examples. The text refers to additional datasets and supplementary implementation details, but none are present in the supplied manuscript.

The evaluation lacks variance over generation seeds and detector training runs, statistical significance, runtime/memory analysis, and sufficient training details for the downstream U-Net. It is therefore unclear how stable the reported gains are or what computational cost is incurred by two diffusion trajectories and per-input prompt optimization.

The prompt-refinement formulation is insufficiently justified. L_ctx pulls all non-anomaly tokens toward their own centroid rather than explicitly aligning them with corresponding normal-prompt tokens, which can collapse distinct token semantics and does not mathematically support the stated context-alignment interpretation. Its effect is not isolated quantitatively from L_anom.

Novelty is somewhat incremental relative to DiffEdit-style prompt-contrast masks, latent inpainting, Attend-and-Excite-like token strengthening, and masked attention control. The anomaly-generation integration is useful, but comparisons or ablations against simpler DiffEdit and attention-map mask baselines are needed to establish that accumulated latent deltas are the source of the improvement.

Baseline protocol details need clarification. The manuscript alleges that some few-shot methods use test data during training, but does not document precisely which published settings do so. More importantly, consistent data access, detector training, source images, prompts, and generation budgets across baselines are not fully established.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important Algorithms/General problem: generating localized industrial anomalies without real anomaly samples or model fine-tuning.

Delta-denoising attribution is an intuitive way to couple synthesis and mask extraction. Normal-reference initialization, latent inpainting, prompt refinement, and spatial attention biasing form a coherent pipeline.
Experiments cover both MVTec AD and VisA, two diffusion backbones, downstream detection, component ablations, threshold sensitivity, SAM dependence, and computational cost.
The downstream results are encouraging: DeltaDeno generally improves over recent zero-shot generation baselines, while the FLUX variant obtains particularly strong image-level performance.
Qualitative examples show diverse localized defects with paired masks, and the paper openly discusses limitations involving evaluation, fine-grained control, and logical anomalies.
weaknesses: The central novelty is insufficiently distinguished from DiffEdit and related prompt-contrastive diffusion editing. Both derive edit regions by contrasting diffusion behavior under source and target prompts; the paper does not provide a direct adapted DiffEdit baseline or isolate whether trajectory accumulation offers a meaningful advantage over noise-prediction or attention differences.

The evidence does not adequately substantiate the principal claims of photorealism and precise mask-image alignment. Inception Score is poorly suited to industrial anomaly realism, and IC-LPIPS measures diversity rather than fidelity. The average IS advantage is negligible (2.05 versus 2.04), with DeltaDeno losing on several categories. There is no human evaluation, real-distribution metric, or direct mask-image alignment/boundary metric.

The downstream protocol risks benchmark overfitting. Thresholds are analyzed using downstream performance on MVTec AD, apparently involving the test anomalies, and the selected T1=0.6 is not even strongest in Table 6: T1=0.4 gives pixel AP 35.3 versus 30.5. The manuscript does not provide a validation-only selection rule, repeated trials, uncertainty estimates, or sensitivity to the chosen single normal reference.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the stated intention to release code. Important details are missing, including the scheduler and classifier-free guidance settings for SD1.5, number of prompt-refinement iterations, smoothing and mask-cleaning operations, SAM mask-selection procedure, prompt lists by category, random seeds, source-image selection, and downstream U-Net training hyperparameters.

The claimed model-agnostic transfer to FLUX is underexplained. The method is formulated around U-Net cross-attention, whereas FLUX uses a transformer architecture; the appendix gives sampling parameters but does not explain how delta attribution and attention biasing are implemented there. Consequently, the strongest reported variant is difficult to verify.

The prompt-refinement formulation is questionable. L_ctx pulls every non-anomaly token toward their within-prompt mean rather than aligning corresponding shared tokens with the normal prompt, potentially collapsing distinct token semantics and not mathematically implementing the stated context-alignment goal.

Algorithm 1 has a control-flow ambiguity: because the early stage is defined to include t_mid, the `else if t=t_mid` mask-extraction branch may be unreachable. Other notation also leaves unclear whether attribution compares latent states that have already diverged, denoiser predictions as claimed in the abstract, or both.

Comparative fairness remains unclear. The main paper claims identical U-Net architectures and schedules across zero-shot methods, while the appendix discusses prior works using different downstream detectors. It is not sufficiently explicit which baselines were rerun, which numbers were borrowed, and whether all generated data and detector training were controlled identically.

Runtime is reported only as being measured on “a single NVIDIA GPU,” without the GPU model, image resolution, precision, or batch size. The paper also omits a societal-impact discussion relevant to synthetic inspection data, such as detector failure caused by unrealistic defects or unrepresented anomaly modes.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical setting: generating localized industrial anomalies without real anomalous examples or category-specific model fine-tuning.

The overall idea—contrasting synchronized normal- and anomaly-conditioned diffusion trajectories, extracting a spatial mask, and using it for constrained inpainting—is intuitive and relevant to computer vision.
Experiments cover both MVTec AD and VisA, include SD1.5 and FLUX backbones, compare against recent zero-shot methods, and report downstream image- and pixel-level detection metrics.
The appendix discusses limitations of existing anomaly-generation evaluation protocols and provides runtime, SAM-dependence, threshold, and few-shot comparisons.
weaknesses: Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the method is not technically sound as written. Sampling starts at t_start=gamma*T with gamma=0.3, while the early stage is defined as [T,T/2] and the mask is extracted at t_mid=T/2. Thus, for T=100, sampling begins at step 30 and never reaches the stated early stage or step 50, so M_mid cannot be constructed. Moreover, Algorithm 1 checks the early-stage condition before the t=t_mid condition even though t_mid is included in the stated early-stage interval, making the mask-extraction branch unreachable under that definition. This central contradiction prevents reproduction of the claimed pipeline.

The paper alternately describes its attribution signal as a difference between denoiser predictions and, in Eq. 8, a difference between already-diverged branch latents. These are materially different quantities; the latter also conflates prompt effects with accumulated trajectory divergence. This undermines the technical interpretation of the core contribution.

Originality relative to DiffEdit is insufficiently established. Both methods contrast source/target prompt-conditioned diffusion behavior to infer an edit mask and then perform localized editing. Adding accumulation, prompt-embedding optimization, SAM priors, and attention biasing appears incremental without a controlled comparison against DiffEdit-style attribution or other plausible mask estimators.

The main claims of precise mask-image alignment and photorealism are not directly evaluated. Inception Score is a poor realism measure for industrial imagery and has no real-image reference, while higher LPIPS can reflect undesirable background changes as easily as useful defect diversity. The appendix itself acknowledges that mask-image pair quality is not measured, yet the paper repeatedly claims precise masks.

The quantitative narrative overstates the evidence. DeltaDeno does not consistently obtain the best IS in Table 1, losing to competitors in many categories. On VisA, FLUX has lower mean pixel AP than AnoStyler, and several categories exhibit very low pixel AP. The SD1.5 result provides only modest average gains and sometimes substantial regressions.

Thresholds are selected using downstream performance on MVTec AD, apparently on the same benchmark test anomalies used for final reporting. With no validation protocol or nested selection described, Table 6 suggests test-set tuning. Prompt descriptions are also given only as examples or 'similar variants,' leaving open category- or test-informed manual selection.

Experimental reliability is weak: there are no repeated trials, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests despite using one normal source image per category and stochastic generation/training. The source-image selection, complete prompt list, baseline reproduction procedure, and VisA split protocol are not adequately specified.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The prompt-refinement iteration count is omitted; 'clean' and smoothing operations are undefined; the detailed U-Net training architecture, optimizer, losses, schedule, and resolution are missing; and the code URL is blank. The context-alignment loss also collapses all non-anomaly token embeddings toward their own centroid rather than aligning them with corresponding normal-prompt tokens, contrary to the stated rationale.

The claimed model-agnostic transfer to FLUX is unsupported technically. FLUX differs substantially from the SD1.5 U-Net/cross-attention formulation, yet the paper does not explain how delta attribution and token-specific attention biasing are implemented for it. The FLUX configuration also changes the number of steps and noise strength, so the comparison does not isolate backbone transfer.

The ablations omit the central design choices: latent-difference accumulation versus denoiser-difference attribution, synchronized-noise controls, normal-reference initialization, SAM foreground masking, accumulation schedule, and comparison with attention-map or DiffEdit masks. Consequently, the experiments do not establish that delta-denoising attribution itself causes the reported gains.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/eaee06c0995c4483aaf4885c28d60088/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses a practically important setting: generating localized industrial anomalies without real defects, pixel annotations, or generator fine-tuning. This is well motivated and relevant to computer vision deployment.

The synchronized normal/anomalous diffusion branches provide an intuitive mechanism for obtaining an image-specific edit region. Combining this attribution with reference-guided initialization and masked latent inpainting is coherent and produces visually plausible local edits in the supplied examples.

The downstream results are promising. On MVTec AD, DeltaDeno-SD1.5 improves mean image AUROC from 77.6 to 84.7 and pixel AUROC from 83.3 to 84.9 relative to AnomalyAny; the FLUX variant reaches 89.7 image AUROC and 41.5 pixel AP. Results on VisA provide useful evidence beyond a single dataset.

The evaluation includes category-level results, component ablations, threshold sensitivity, SAM dependence, computational cost, two diffusion backbones, and extensive qualitative examples. The SAM-free experiment is particularly helpful because it shows that the core method remains functional without the foreground model.

The paper is generally well organized and explicitly discusses limitations of existing generation metrics, detector-confounded evaluation, mask-image pair assessment, and difficulty generating logical anomalies.
weaknesses: There is a serious inconsistency in the sampling schedule. The method initializes at t_start=gamma*T with gamma=0.3 and T=100, hence at timestep 30, but defines the early stage as [T,T/2] and extracts M_mid at floor(T/2)=50. A reverse trajectory from 30 to 0 never reaches 50, so Algorithm 1 cannot operate as written. If t denotes an iteration index rather than the diffusion timestep, the equations and implementation details must be reformulated unambiguously.

The main novelty over DiffEdit and related prompt-contrastive editing is insufficiently isolated. DiffEdit already derives masks by contrasting source and target prompts under a shared diffusion schedule; SAM-based spatial restriction, attention-logit biasing, and blended latent inpainting are also established ideas. The paper needs a sharper conceptual and empirical comparison with DiffEdit adapted to anomaly generation.

The evidence does not substantiate the strongest realism and mask-precision claims. Inception Score does not compare generated images with real anomalies and is not a reliable measure of photorealism; IC-LPIPS measures diversity rather than fidelity. The average IS improvement over AnoStyler is only 2.05 versus 2.04 and DeltaDeno is worse in several categories. Despite emphasizing paired mask quality, the paper supplies no direct human study or quantitative mask-image alignment evaluation.

The downstream protocol is underspecified and internally unclear. The main text describes evaluation on the real test split, whereas the appendix says that only the remaining two-thirds of MVTec AD are evaluated to accommodate few-shot baselines. It is unclear whether Tables 2 and 5 use identical splits, how the VisA split is formed, whether baseline results were reimplemented under exactly the same detector recipe, or how reference images were selected. No multi-seed variation or statistical uncertainty is reported.

Several implementation details required for reproduction are absent: the SD sampler and guidance scale, prompt-refinement iteration count, complete per-category anomaly prompts, mask smoothing/cleanup operations, attention layers modified, random-seed protocol, and downstream U-Net losses and training schedule. The promised code link is blank in the manuscript.

The prompt-refinement formulation does not match its stated motivation. L_ctx pulls every non-anomaly token toward their within-prompt centroid rather than aligning shared tokens with the normal prompt; this can collapse distinct token semantics and does not mathematically ensure that differences are confined to the anomaly token.

Hyperparameter selection may be entangled with test evaluation. Table 6 shows that T1=0.4 substantially improves pixel AP over the chosen T1=0.6 setting (35.3 versus 30.5), while the manuscript says defaults were chosen from these observations without identifying a validation set. This raises the possibility of benchmark-test tuning.

Overall, the idea and empirical trends are encouraging, but the contradictory core schedule and inadequate validation of realism/mask accuracy leave the scientific case just short of acceptance under an Algorithms/General assessment.
